rq1_individual_baselines.question: How accurately can individual machine-learning algorithms detect malicious network traffic?
rq1_individual_baselines.finding: With default hyperparameters, xgboost was the strongest single model (test F1 0.9975, recall 0.9975, 3-fold CV F1 0.9897 ± 0.0027); logistic regression was weakest (F1 0.8431). Tree-based models separate attack flows far better than a linear boundary.

rq2_feature_selection.question: Does feature selection / dimensionality reduction improve model performance and training efficiency?
rq2_feature_selection.finding: Using all 70 features, Random Forest reached F1 0.9951 in 0.49s. The best reduced set, correlation_filter_0.90 (37 features), reached F1 0.9938 (-0.0013) with training time +36%. Fastest configuration: all_features (0.49s, F1 0.9951).

rq3_optimization_impact.question: How do optimized models compare with their unoptimized versions, and how do Grid, Random and Bayesian search compare?
rq3_optimization_impact.finding: Optuna tuning improved the test F1 of random forest from 0.9951 to 0.9963 (+0.12%). Across search strategies on Random Forest, RandomizedSearchCV found the best CV F1 (0.9835) and GridSearchCV was fastest (5s); for XGBoost, GridSearchCV found the best CV F1 (0.9907). On this well-separated data the gains from tuning are small in absolute terms; the differences show up mostly in false-negative rate and in search cost.

rq4_ensemble_superiority.question: Do ensemble methods outperform individual classifiers?
rq4_ensemble_superiority.finding: The best ensemble, stacking (Stacking), scored F1 0.9988 versus 0.9975 for the best single model (xgboost), a difference of +0.0013. 1 of 7 ensembles beat the best single model. Ensembles give a consistent but small edge here because the strongest single learners are already near the ceiling; the clearer benefit is lower variance (see bootstrap CIs) and fewer missed rare attacks.

rq5_optimal_tradeoff.question: Which model provides the best trade-off between detection, false alarms and latency?
rq5_optimal_tradeoff.finding: Models within 0.002 F1 of the best (0.9988) were: xgboost, stacking. Among them xgboost is the recommended deployment choice (3.23 ms per 1k flows). Highest attack recall: stacking (0.9975); lowest false-positive rate: stacking (0.0000).

rq6_explainability.question: Can the final model provide interpretable explanations for why traffic was classified as malicious?
rq6_explainability.finding: SHAP (TreeExplainer) on optimized xgboost ranks Destination Port, Init_Win_bytes_forward and Bwd Packet Length Min as the strongest global drivers. These are flow-shape statistics (packet sizes, timing, window sizes) rather than identifiers, which is consistent with the model learning attack behaviour instead of memorising addresses.

rq7_imbalance_handling.question: Which imbalanced-data strategy works best: nothing, class weighting, under-sampling or SMOTE?
rq7_imbalance_handling.finding: The training split is 26.7% attack. For logistic regression, recall moved from 0.8133 (no handling) to 0.9509 with class weights and 0.9459 with SMOTE, at FPR 0.0613 / 0.1134 / 0.1089. Best strategy per model (by F1): logistic regression -> smote, decision tree -> class_weight, random forest -> none. Tree ensembles are far less sensitive to the imbalance than the linear model.

rq8_per_attack_type.question: Which attack categories does the best model still miss?
rq8_per_attack_type.finding: All attack categories in the test split were detected with recall >= 0.95.

executive_summary: On a class-capped stratified sample of the real CIC-IDS2017 corpus, the best detector was stacking (F1 0.9988, recall 0.9975, FPR 0.0000). Hyperparameter tuning changed the best single model's F1 by +0.12%; the best ensemble differed from the best single model by +0.0013 F1. All attack categories in the test split were detected with recall >= 0.
